clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia in which lower-limb spasticity is combined with amyotrophy of the small hand muscles
Caused by heterozygous variants in BSCL2, which encodes seipin, an endoplasmic reticulum protein involved in lipid-droplet biology
The wasting characteristically begins in the thenar eminence and first dorsal interosseous, giving prominent intrinsic-hand-muscle atrophy
Marked intrafamilial variability is typical, with some carriers showing predominantly spasticity and others predominantly distal wasting
BSCL2 is allelic with distal hereditary motor neuropathy type V and with Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2, and different BSCL2 variants cause congenital generalised lipodystrophy
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography confirm a motor axonopathy affecting the hands and feet
Care is symptomatic, combining physiotherapy, spasticity control and hand-function support with occupational therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Silver syndrome results from dominant variants in BSCL2, the gene for seipin, an integral endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein important for lipid-droplet formation and endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis. The classical Silver syndrome variants (such as N88S and S90L) are thought to disturb glycosylation and cause misfolded seipin to accumulate, triggering endoplasmic reticulum stress and a toxic gain of function in motor neurons. This preferentially injures the longest corticospinal tracts and distal motor axons supplying the hands and feet, producing the distinctive combination of lower-limb spasticity with intrinsic-hand-muscle amyotrophy. Separate loss-of-function BSCL2 variants instead cause a lipodystrophy phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Distal hereditary motor neuropathy type V (allelic BSCL2 disease)
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs
SPG10 (KIF5A) complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia with amyotrophy
Hirayama disease and other focal motor neuronopathies
additionalInvestigations: BSCL2 sequencing within a hereditary spastic paraplegia or inherited neuropathy panel
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to define the motor axonopathy
MRI of brain and cervical spine to exclude compressive and demyelinating causes
Detailed family history given wide phenotypic variability
Assessment of hand function and grip for rehabilitation planning
Screening for metabolic features to distinguish lipodystrophy-associated BSCL2 variants
redFlags: Bulbar symptoms or brisk spread of weakness suggesting motor neurone disease
A cervical sensory level or radicular pain pointing to compressive myeloradiculopathy
Rapidly progressive respiratory or swallowing difficulty
Severe distal weakness threatening loss of independent hand function
reference.prognosis: Progression is usually slow, and although hand-muscle wasting can cause meaningful disability, many affected people retain ambulation and useful function for prolonged periods; severity varies considerably even within a family.
pitfalls: Attributing intrinsic-hand-muscle wasting to a local entrapment neuropathy rather than the underlying genetic disorder
Confusing the neuropathic BSCL2 phenotype with the unrelated lipodystrophy caused by different BSCL2 variants
Assuming a pure hereditary spastic paraplegia when subtle distal amyotrophy is present
Underestimating variability and reassuring at-risk relatives inappropriately
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Antispasticity therapy for the lower-limb spasticity with agents such as baclofen or tizanidine, and focal botulinum toxin injection for targeted muscle overactivity
Physiotherapy and stretching programmes to maintain gait and prevent contractures, with occupational therapy and adaptive aids for the intrinsic-hand-muscle wasting
Ankle-foot orthoses and mobility aids to preserve ambulation and independence
Foot care and orthopaedic management of secondary deformity
Nerve conduction studies, electromyography and functional assessments to characterise the motor axonopathy and monitor progression
Coordinated neurology and rehabilitation input including physiotherapy and occupational therapy
Genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant BSCL2 variant, noting marked intrafamilial variability and the allelic neuropathy and lipodystrophy phenotypes
